Sam Rivera, senior data engineer. Notes for the interview.

MOST RECENT: Harbor Freight Logistics, Mar 2024 to now (contract through Aston). Shipment-event pipeline: carriers send tracking events, we turn them into one status per parcel for the customer-service team. They were answering "where is my parcel" calls by hand, 40 minutes a call, because three carrier feeds disagreed. I joined in March 2024; team of 5 (3 internal, 2 contract, me one of the contract). I built the event adapter for carrier B and the dedupe stage alone; the status rules were shared with Priya. I did not build the carrier A adapter (Priya's) or the customer-service UI. About 2 million events a day across 11 depots. Production since June 2024. Chose Kafka over SQS because we needed replay when a carrier resent a day of events; the team lead wanted SQS for simplicity and his argument was that nobody on the team had run Kafka. Dedupe key is carrier id plus parcel id plus event time. Validated by running old and new side by side for six weeks. In August a carrier changed its timestamp format, the dedupe stage dropped 3 percent of events for two days; found by the customer-service team, not by us. Cost: two days of wrong statuses. Would add schema checks at the adapter edge. Engagement is going well, they have asked me to stay.

EARLIER: Brightwell Insurance, Jan 2021 to Feb 2024. Claims intake portal for adjusters, so they stop re-keying paper forms. I owned the document-upload service and the form-validation rules. One decision I can defend: we stored uploads in S3 with metadata in Postgres rather than putting the files in the database, because files were up to 80 MB and backups were already slow. Technologies: Python and FastAPI for the upload service, S3 presigned URLs so the browser uploaded directly, Postgres for metadata, Terraform for the buckets and roles.

EARLIER: Cobalt Retail, Jun 2018 to Dec 2020. Inventory sync between stores and the web shop. I wrote the nightly reconciliation job. Decision: a nightly batch instead of streaming, because stores had unreliable connections and the business only needed next-morning accuracy. Technologies: Java and Spring Batch for the job, MySQL for the store tables, and Jenkins for the nightly schedule.
